subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'community' in an ecosystem?
options: All the populations of different species living in the same habitat
All the members of one species living in a habitat
The living and non-living parts of a habitat together
A single organism and its immediate surroundings
questions.explain: A community is all the populations of the different species that live and interact in the same habitat.

questions.q: Which term describes all the individuals of a single species living in a particular area?
options: Population
Community
Ecosystem
Biosphere
questions.explain: A population is all the organisms of one species living in the same place at the same time.

questions.q: Which of the following is an abiotic factor that could affect the distribution of organisms?
options: Light intensity
Availability of prey
Competition for mates
Presence of predators
questions.explain: Abiotic factors are non-living conditions such as light intensity, temperature and soil pH.

questions.q: In a food web, the number of rabbits falls sharply. What is the most likely immediate effect on the foxes that eat them?
options: The fox population is likely to decrease
The fox population is likely to increase
The foxes will begin to photosynthesise
The foxes will become producers
questions.explain: Interdependence means fewer prey provide less food, so the predator population tends to fall.

questions.q: A student counts an average of 8 daisies per 1 m2 quadrat in a field measuring 400 m2. What is the best estimate of the total number of daisies?
questions.explain: Estimated total = mean per m2 x total area = 8 x 400 = 3200.

questions.q: What is a quadrat mainly used to investigate?
options: The distribution and abundance of organisms
The mass of individual animals
The rate of respiration in plants
The pH of soil samples
questions.explain: Quadrats are used to sample the abundance and distribution of slow-moving or non-moving organisms.

questions.q: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in the root nodules of legumes and receive sugars from the plant while supplying it with nitrogen compounds. This relationship is an example of:
options: Mutualism
Parasitism
Predation
Competition
questions.explain: Mutualism is a relationship in which both organisms benefit.

questions.q: What does biodiversity measure?
options: The variety of different species in an ecosystem
The total mass of one species
The number of abiotic factors present
The rate of nutrient cycling
questions.explain: Biodiversity is the variety of different species of organisms within an ecosystem or on Earth.

questions.q: Why is a high biodiversity generally beneficial to an ecosystem?
options: It makes the ecosystem more stable and resistant to change
It reduces the number of food chains present
It prevents any nutrient cycling from occurring
It guarantees that no species can ever go extinct
questions.explain: Greater biodiversity increases stability by ensuring species are less dependent on any single other species.

questions.q: Why do reforestation programmes help to maintain biodiversity?
options: They restore habitats, providing homes and food for more species
They remove all decomposers from the soil
They increase the rate of combustion of fossil fuels
They reduce the amount of photosynthesis in an area
questions.explain: Replanting trees rebuilds habitats and food sources, supporting a wider range of species.

questions.q: Fertiliser runs off a field into a lake, causing an algal bloom. Why do fish in the lake then begin to die?
options: Decomposers respire and deplete the dissolved oxygen in the water
The algae directly poison the fish with nitrates
The water temperature rises above boiling point
Sunlight increases the oxygen concentration too much
questions.explain: In eutrophication, plants die and decomposers use up dissolved oxygen as they respire, suffocating aquatic animals.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
options: Photosynthesis
Respiration
Combustion
Decomposition
questions.explain: Plants and algae take in atmospheric carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.

questions.q: Which two processes both return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
options: Respiration and combustion
Photosynthesis and condensation
Evaporation and precipitation
Nitrification and denitrification
questions.explain: Respiration by organisms and the burning (combustion) of fuels both release carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What is the role of decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, in the carbon cycle?
options: They break down dead organisms, releasing carbon dioxide through respiration
They fix carbon dioxide directly into glucose
They convert nitrates into nitrogen gas
They cause water to evaporate from oceans
questions.explain: Decomposers respire as they break down dead matter, returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which process transfers water vapour from the leaves of plants into the atmosphere?
options: Transpiration
Condensation
Precipitation
Combustion
questions.explain: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves, contributing to the water cycle.

questions.q: A coastal region has plenty of seawater but little fresh water. How can distillation be used to produce potable water?
options: Water is evaporated and the vapour condensed, leaving the salts behind
Salt is added to the water to make it drinkable
The water is frozen to remove the dissolved oxygen
Nitrogen gas is bubbled through the water
questions.explain: Distillation boils seawater and condenses the pure vapour, separating fresh water from dissolved salts.

questions.q: What do nitrogen-fixing bacteria do in the nitrogen cycle?
options: Convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds such as ammonia
Convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas
Break down proteins into carbon dioxide
Turn nitrates into oxygen
questions.explain: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert unreactive atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds.

questions.q: Nitrifying bacteria in well-aerated soil carry out which conversion?
options: Ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates
Nitrates into nitrogen gas
Nitrogen gas into ammonia
Proteins into amino acids
questions.explain: Nitrification is the oxidation of ammonia to nitrites and then to nitrates by nitrifying bacteria.

questions.q: What do denitrifying bacteria do, particularly in waterlogged soils?
options: Convert nitrates into nitrogen gas
Convert nitrogen gas into ammonia
Convert ammonia into nitrates
Convert glucose into carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrates to nitrogen gas, reducing soil fertility, especially in anaerobic waterlogged soil.

questions.q: A farmer grows a crop of legumes such as clover and then ploughs it back into the field. Why does this increase soil fertility?
options: Root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria that add nitrogen compounds to the soil
The legumes remove all nitrates from the soil
The plants convert nitrates directly into nitrogen gas
The crop increases denitrification in the soil
questions.explain: Legume root nodules house nitrogen-fixing bacteria, so ploughing them in enriches the soil with nitrogen compounds.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Biology (1BI0) specification; Ecosystems & Material Cycles
